summary: This note describes how the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is organized and operates, and it corrects a notable error. The IPCC's summary for policymakers included a projection about Himalayan glacier melt dated 2035 that was not in the final summary; the IPCC later acknowledged the date was incorrect while affirming the conclusion. The note also explains the roles of chapter authors (coordinating lead, lead, and contributing) and how panel membership, plenary sessions, and meeting attendance are structured.
one_line: Describes the IPCC's 2035 glacier-date error and how its chapter authors, government representatives, and plenary sessions are structured.
key_facts: The IPCC acknowledged that a 2035 projection was incorrect but reaffirmed that the conclusion in its final summary for policymakers was robust.
The IPCC expressed regret for "the poor application of well-established IPCC procedures in this instance".

The date of 2035 was correctly quoted by the IPCC from a WWF report, which had misquoted its own source, an ICSI report titled "Variations of Snow and Ice in the past and at present on a Global and Regional Scale".
A projection with the 2035 date was not included in the final summary for policymakers.
Each IPCC chapter typically has two "coordinating lead authors", ten to fifteen "lead authors", and a somewhat larger number of "contributing authors".
Coordinating lead authors assemble the contributions of other authors, ensure they meet stylistic and formatting requirements, and report to the Working Group chairs.
Lead authors are responsible for writing sections of chapters.
Contributing authors prepare text, graphs or data for inclusion by the lead authors.
The IPCC Panel is composed of representatives appointed by governments and organizations, and participation of delegates with appropriate expertise is encouraged.
Plenary sessions of the IPCC and its Working Groups are held at the level of government representatives.
Non Governmental and Intergovernmental Organizations may be allowed to attend plenary sessions as observers.
Sessions of the IPCC Bureau, workshops, and expert and lead authors meetings are by invitation only.
Attendance at the 2003 meeting included 350 government officials and climate change experts.
The meeting report states there were 322 persons in attendance at Sessions, with about seven-eighths of participants from governmental organizations.
